newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends lower in US, Japan trade, Dow slide weigh.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends lower in US, Japan trade, Dow slide weigh.

text.p: The dollar retreated from a new 41-month high versus the mark, ending slightly lower overall, with support eroded by a jump in Japan's current account surplus reported overnight and a late slide on Wall Street.
"The dollar is being dragged down at the close with the underperformance of the stock market," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
The Dow Jones industrial average was down almost 170 points during the afternoon and closed down almost 120 points.
The dollar ended at 112.71/81 yen, down from 112.80/85 at the open and at 1.7598/08 marks, off from 1.7617/20.

Earlier, Japan reported that its May current account surplus, often a source of friction with the United States, jumped 154.9 percent to 906.8 billion yen. Although near market expectations, the figures eventually weighed on the dollar.
"It backed off on the realization that it is still a widening trade surplus," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange trading manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

Japanese economists and Finance officials have expressed the view that the surging surplus was due to a hefty increase in exports, which rose 20 percent in May, notably car sales to the United States.
U.S. manufacturers continue to complain that their competitive edge has been eroded by a strong dollar this year.

Remarks at a San Francisco meeting of the Japan-U.S. Business Council on Tuesday from Ford Motor Co vice chairman Wayne Booker also pressured the U.S. currency. Booker called for a weaker dollar, targeting a 100 to 110 yen exchange rate.
Late on Wednesday further remarks from U.S. and Japanese business leaders called for exchange rate stability.

The dollar's decline was surprisingly subdued and Japanese officials were quick to say the flood of exports would soon be counterbalanced by a pickup in imports after the effects of a recent consumer tax hike wear off, dealers said.
Mark/yen also showed resilience, clambering back over 64.00, after touching a fresh 23-month low at 63.89 in early dealings.

"With the actual number coming in pretty much with people's expectations, plus the comments from Ministry of Finance officials indicating it was just a temporary fluctuation ... it really did temper concern that you could get a reignition of the trade war," said Anne Pankowski, a vice president at CIBC Wood Gundy.

In early New York trade, the dollar rose to 1.7655 marks, its highest since February 1994, mostly as a result of continued mark selling by investors concerned that Europe will replace the German currency with a broad-based, but weak single currency as planned in 1999.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4582/92 Swiss francs from 1.4630/40 Swiss at the open. It rose to Canadian $1.3740/45 from C$1.3734/39.
The pound rose to $1.6870/80 from $1.6845/55, with activity dampened while the markets awaited the outcome of the Bank of England's two day monetary policy meeting on Thursday.
The Australian dollar eased to $0.7436/41 from $0.7439/44.
